purpose: One set of examples for the two implementations that read a stored record heading as plain text, so the title the server prints in the page head, the link preview and the plain article page is the text the app shows for the same heading. Every expected value was produced by running readInlineHeadingText in the frontend test DOM. Inputs on which that DOM and real browsers disagree are left out on purpose: noscript, dialog and search inside wrongly nested tags, text placed directly inside a table, tags inside select, and a stray end tag after nothing but title or noframes. How the server reads some of those is pinned in its own test, public_article_heading_text_test.go.

headingText.why: Plain text stays as it is.
Without markup only the two ends are trimmed.
An ampersand in plain text is left alone.
A bare type parameter is not markup, so it stays (an earlier server reader returned "Vector").
A less-than sign in ordinary text is not markup.
A closing tag alone is not markup.
Without markup a character reference is not decoded.
An ampersand and a heart stay as typed.
A lone unsupported tag with no closing tag anywhere stays visible.
A comment alone is not markup, so it stays visible.
Escaped tags are not markup and stay escaped.
A tag name cut off at the very end is not markup.
A dot in the tag name fails the markup test, so the text stays.
A slash alone after a tag name does not make it markup; "/>" or ">" would.
Without markup an inner line break is kept.
Without markup a Windows line ending is kept as it is.
Whitespace alone reads as nothing.
Finnish letters pass through untouched.
No-break spaces at the two ends are trimmed (JavaScript whitespace); the one inside stays.
Ideographic spaces at the two ends are trimmed too.
A byte-order mark at the start is whitespace in JavaScript (Go's TrimSpace would keep it).
The next-line character U+0085 is not whitespace in JavaScript, so it stays (Go's TrimSpace would remove it).
Letter case does not matter for the tags the app renders.
An upper-case tag the app renders is markup by itself, with no closing tag anywhere.
A space between "<" and the tag name still counts as markup: the parser finds no tag, but the character reference is decoded.
A no-break space after the tag name is whitespace for the markup test (JavaScript's \s), although the parser then sees an unknown tag.
So is a vertical tab, which the parser takes for part of the tag name: an unknown tag, so no space is added.
A no-break space after "script" passes the test for hidden tags; the parser then sees an unknown tag, and its content stays.
A complete unsupported element is markup: its tags go and no space is added.
A colon in the name of an unsupported element: still markup.
A hyphen in the name, as in a custom element: still markup.
A no-break space after the name of an unsupported tag is whitespace for the markup test too.
With a closing tag somewhere, a bare type parameter becomes an unknown tag and disappears.
"<b " followed by more words opens a tag that never ends, so the rest is lost.
The long s is not an ASCII s for the rendered tags, so this is not markup and nothing is decoded (Go's (?i) would call it markup).
For the hidden tags the long s does count as s, so this is markup: the parser finds no tag, but the character reference is decoded.
JavaScript lower-cases the Kelvin sign to k, so this unknown tag still separates words like a blockquote.
An inline tag adds no space (an earlier server reader returned "Travel deals !").
An inline tag inside CJK text adds no space (an earlier server reader put spaces between the characters).
Spaces around an inline tag are kept as they are.
Neighbouring inline elements are not separated.
Nested inline tags add nothing.
A link keeps its text.
A link the app refuses to make clickable still keeps its text.
Pasted word-processor markup: unknown tags vanish without a trace.
A heading wrapper is removed.
A real stored heading: wrapper removed, character reference decoded.

headingText.why: Neighbouring blocks get one space.
One space between a heading and a paragraph; the inline tags inside add none.
The space between blocks is an ordinary space, also between CJK blocks.
Blocks inside a heading separate words too.
List items are blocks.
A boundary where a nested block starts and where it ends.
Text after a block gets the space.
A quotation is a block.
A line break tag separates words.
A self-closing line break inside a heading.
A rule line separates words.
A rich-text editor's trailing empty paragraph leaves nothing behind.
Sectioning tags are not among the rendered tags, so they add no space.
Table cells that are opened and closed in order read in order, with no space between cells.
A pasted whole document: html and body tags are ignored.
No space is added when the text before the boundary already ends with whitespace.
No space is added when the text after the boundary starts with whitespace.
Both original spaces stay and none is added: nothing is collapsed.
A line break between two blocks is kept and takes the place of the space.
A blank line between blocks survives.
A no-break space counts as whitespace at a boundary, so no space is added.
The ideographic space counts as whitespace at a boundary.
A byte-order mark between blocks counts as whitespace (Go's unicode.IsSpace says otherwise).
U+0085 is not whitespace in JavaScript, so the space is added (Go's unicode.IsSpace says otherwise).
The zero-width space is not whitespace, so the space is added.
Inner spaces and line breaks are kept; only the two ends are trimmed.
Whitespace inside and outside the heading tag is trimmed at the two ends.
An inner tab is kept.
JavaScript-only whitespace at the two ends of marked-up text is trimmed.
An emoji, a character outside the basic plane, before a boundary.
A heading that holds only whitespace reads as nothing.
An empty heading reads as nothing.
A lone line break tag reads as nothing.
A lone no-break space inside a paragraph is trimmed away.
Named, decimal and hexadecimal character references; a no-break space inside the text is kept.
Finnish text with references: the no-break spaces inside stay.
Escaped tags inside markup become literal characters, not tags.
A no-break space written as a reference is trimmed at the two ends.
Old references work without their semicolon; an unknown name stays as typed.
A reference that stands for two characters (Go's html package leaves this one out).
A reference is decoded once, not twice.
A reference cut in two by a tag is no reference.
A numeric reference without digits is no reference and stays as typed (Go's html package returns U+FFFD).
A one-digit numeric reference at the end of a text is decoded without its semicolon (Go's html package leaves it).
A number beyond the last character becomes the replacement character U+FFFD (Go's html package wraps it round to "A").
A literal less-than sign beside real markup.
Literal "<" and ">" beside real markup and a reference.
A script is dropped with its content.
An unclosed script takes the rest of the text with it.
A style element is dropped; nothing is left.
Style in either letter case is dropped and separates nothing.
Tags inside script text are not tags.
Inside a script's "<!--", an inner "<script>" hides the next "</script>".
A template is dropped with its content.
An unclosed template takes the rest with it.
Templates nest: the inner end tag does not end the outer template.
A comment is dropped and separates nothing; a tag inside it is no tag.
A comment between blocks: the space comes from the blocks.
An unfinished comment hides the rest.
A comment also ends at "--!>".
"<!-->" and "<!--->" are complete comments.
A document type line and a processing instruction are dropped.
A CDATA section is a comment in HTML and is dropped.
An end tag without a name vanishes.
A ">" inside a quoted attribute value does not end the tag, with either kind of quote.
Without quotes the first ">" ends the tag.
A quote that does not follow an equals sign is no quote for the parser.
A line break inside a tag belongs to the tag.
Attribute text is never read, not even the description of an image.
Title content is text: the reference is decoded, the inner tag stays as typed.
Textarea content is text and is kept as typed.
Iframe content is text exactly as typed: nothing is decoded.
After "<plaintext>" everything is text, even its own end tag.
The parser drops a line break right after "<pre>".
Only the first line break after "<pre>" is dropped.
The same line break is dropped after "<textarea>".
With markup the parser turns a Windows line ending into a line feed.
An unclosed element is closed at the end.
An unfinished tag at the end is discarded.
"</" at the very end is text.
A new paragraph closes the open one.
A new list item ends the open one; the second end tag is then stray, so "c" and "d" stay together.

A stray "

" after the first start tag stands for an empty paragraph, which is a word boundary.
A stray "</br>" is read as a line break.
Any other stray end tag is ignored: no boundary.

Before the first start tag every end tag is ignored, even "

".
A heading inside a heading ends the outer one; its late end tag is then stray, so "c" and "d" stay together.
An end tag of any heading level ends the open heading.

A sectioning tag ends an open paragraph without separating words itself; the late "

" is then a boundary of its own.
An inline end tag cannot close a block that was opened inside it.
The end tag of a list item does not reach past an inner list.
Overlapping inline and block tags: the paragraph ends where its end tag stands.
A link inside a link ends the outer one, so no link is open after the end tag: the second heading directly follows the first and ends it, and the late "" is stray.
An inline end tag ends its element even while a block opened inside it is still open, and the block stays open. With the bold gone, the second heading again ends the first.
That inline end tag also ends the ordinary tags inside the open block: here the Kelvin-sign tag the browser reads as a quotation, whose end separates the words.
